title: Uncertainty-Aware Motion Planning for Autonomous Driving in Mixed Traffic Environment
summary: In mixed-traffic environments where autonomous and human-driven vehicles may co-exist, motion planning for autonomous vehicles requires anticipating the future behaviors of surrounding human drivers. Existing reinforcement learning-based methods generally directly incorporate the predicted human intents into the observation to enable a proactive planning. However, human intent is inherently uncertain due to the behavioral diversity, perception noise, and partial observability. Treating predicted intends as deterministic states can result in unsafe decisions for autonomous vehicles. To address this problem, we propose Uncertainty-Aware Motion Planning (UAMP), which incorporates uncertainty in human intent prediction for AV decision-making. Specifically, UAMP first introduces a proximity-aware uncertainty estimator to quantify the interaction-conditioned intent uncertainty and constructs an uncertainty-guided joint intent distribution over surrounding human-driven vehicles. Within this uncertainty set, UAMP further introduces Uncertainty-Calibrated Value Learning (UCVL) to correct value function learning biases arising from directly incorporating uncertain human intent predictions into the observation. Extensive experiments in various mixed-traffic scenarios show that UAMP significantly improves safety and driving comfort, while maintaining traffic efficiency compared with existing approaches. The code is released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/UAMP-5638.

AI.tldr: UAMP integrates uncertainty-aware intent prediction and uncertainty-calibrated value learning to improve safety and comfort of autonomous vehicles in mixed-traffic environments.
AI.motivation: Existing RL-based motion planning methods directly incorporate predicted human intents as deterministic states, but human intent is inherently uncertain due to behavioral diversity, perception noise, and partial observability. Treating predicted intents as deterministic can lead to unsafe decisions for autonomous vehicles.
AI.method: UAMP consists of two main components: (1) a proximity-aware uncertainty estimator that quantifies interaction-conditioned intent uncertainty and constructs an uncertainty-guided joint intent distribution; (2) Uncertainty-Calibrated Value Learning (UCVL) that corrects value function learning biases arising from directly incorporating uncertain human intent predictions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments in various mixed-traffic scenarios demonstrate that UAMP significantly improves safety and driving comfort while maintaining traffic efficiency compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly modeling uncertainty in human intent prediction and calibrating value function learning, UAMP enables autonomous vehicles to make safer and more robust motion planning decisions in mixed-traffic environments.

title: On the Controllability-Fidelity Frontier in Diffusion Editing
summary: Diffusion-based generative models enable powerful image editing capabilities, but achieving precise control while maintaining fidelity and safety remains challenging. We present a comprehensive theoretical and empirical study of controllable diffusion-based image editing, analyzing the trade-offs between adherence to user intent, preservation of non-target content, and output quality. Our work spans text- and mask-guided edits, point/drag manipulation, and inversion-based pipelines. We derive mathematical formulations of editing objectives and analyze dynamics of noise injection, score guidance, and inversion error. We provide theoretical bounds on reconstruction error, stability under repeated edits, and locality of changes. We propose algorithmic frameworks (with pseudocode) for mask-localized and instruction-guided editing, and present extensive experiments comparing state-of-the-art methods (e.g.\ TF-ICON \cite{lu2023tficone}, DragFlow \cite{zhou2025dragflow}, InstructPix2Pix \cite{brooks2023instructpix2pix}, UltraEdit \cite{zhao2024ultraedit}) on multiple tasks and metrics (FID, identity similarity, CLIP alignment, artifact scores, etc). Our results reveal key failure modes, such as identity drift, prompt sensitivity, and compositional errors. We also discuss ethical considerations in image editing, including misuse risks, bias, consent, and concept erasure techniques (e.g.\ MACE \cite{lu2024mace}, ANT \cite{li2025ant}, EraseAnything \cite{gao2024eraseanything}) as safeguards. We conclude with best practices and future directions for responsible, high-fidelity diffusion-based editing.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a comprehensive theoretical and empirical study of controllable diffusion-based image editing, analyzing trade-offs between user intent adherence, non-target content preservation, and output quality across various editing methods.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based generative models enable powerful image editing, but achieving precise control while maintaining fidelity and safety remains challenging. There's a need to analyze trade-offs between adherence to user intent, preservation of non-target content, and output quality.
AI.method: The authors derive mathematical formulations of editing objectives and analyze noise injection, score guidance, and inversion error dynamics. They propose algorithmic frameworks for mask-localized and instruction-guided editing with pseudocode. They conduct extensive experiments comparing state-of-the-art methods (TF-ICON, DragFlow, InstructPix2Pix, UltraEdit) on multiple tasks and metrics (FID, identity similarity, CLIP alignment, artifact scores).
AI.result: Their results reveal key failure modes including identity drift, prompt sensitivity, and compositional errors. They provide theoretical bounds on reconstruction error, stability under repeated edits, and locality of changes. The analysis shows the challenges in maintaining both fidelity and controllability in diffusion-based editing.
AI.conclusion: The paper discusses ethical considerations including misuse risks, bias, consent, and concept erasure techniques (MACE, ANT, EraseAnything). They conclude with best practices and future directions for responsible, high-fidelity diffusion-based editing.

title: GHOST: Hierarchical Sub-Goal Policies for Generalizing Robot Manipulation
summary:
We present GHOST, a framework for learning visuomotor manipulation policies that generalize beyond the training distribution. GHOST factorizes control into (i) a high-level policy that predicts the next sub-goal as a distribution over 3D end-effector poses from multi-view RGB-D observations, and (ii) a low-level goal-conditioned controller that executes embodiment-specific actions. To condition image-based policies on 3D goals, we introduce a simple spatial interface that projects predicted goals into the image plane and represents them as end-effector heatmaps. Across a suite of manipulation tasks, this hierarchical factorization consistently improves performance and robustness compared to a flat Diffusion Policy.
  Further, we show that this hierarchical interface also makes it easy to incorporate human demonstrations without relying on (noisy) action retargeting. As sub-goals are largely embodiment-agnostic, we train the high-level policy on human video to specify how learned skills should be applied and composed, while keeping the low-level policy trained purely on robot data. This hierarchy enables adaptation to novel objects and task variations using a small number of human demonstrations.

AI.tldr: GHOST is a hierarchical visuomotor manipulation framework that factorizes control into a high-level goal-predicting policy and low-level goal-conditioned controller, improving generalization and enabling effective human demonstration integration without action retargeting.
AI.motivation: Existing flat diffusion policies struggle with generalization beyond training distribution and require noisy action retargeting to incorporate human demonstrations. The authors seek a framework that generalizes better, incorporates human demonstrations without retargeting, and adapts to novel objects/task variations with minimal demonstrations.
AI.method: GHOST factorizes control hierarchically: (1) a high-level policy predicting next sub-goals as 3D end-effector pose distributions from multi-view RGB-D observations, and (2) a low-level goal-conditioned controller executing embodiment-specific actions. A spatial interface projects predicted goals into the image plane as end-effector heatmaps. The high-level policy is trained on human video to specify skill composition, while the low-level policy is trained on robot data.
AI.result: Across manipulation tasks, the hierarchical factorization consistently improves performance and robustness compared to flat Diffusion Policy. The framework enables easy incorporation of human demonstrations without action retargeting and allows adaptation to novel objects and task variations using small numbers of human demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical approach provides better generalization and robustness than flat policies, effectively leverages human demonstrations without retargeting, and enables rapid adaptation to novel scenarios with minimal demonstration data.

title: Continuous Neural Reparameterization as a Deep Geometric Prior for Robust Fixed-Chart UV Repair
summary: Traditional UV unwrapping relies on direct optimization of geometric distortion energies and can fail through invalid initialization, local minima, or topological foldovers. We recast fixed-chart UV unwrapping as continuous neural reparameterization: an untrained SIREN maps per-vertex mesh features to UV coordinates, and its weights are optimized for a geometric objective. The practical contribution is a robust chart-solver recipe, combining Laplace--Beltrami spectral inputs, Tutte residual warm-up, a $C^2$ determinant extension, an injectivity barrier, and validity-checked retry/fallback routing, rather than a claim that any single component guarantees validity or that recutting methods should be replaced. NTK--LBO diagnostics show that spectral conditioning changes update geometry, especially at initialization and mid-rank subspaces, but does not by itself predict chart success. On compact pre-cut charts and a 47-chart stratified Thingi10K/xatlas-cut benchmark, the neural solver produces zero flips on all compact charts and 42/47 valid zero-flip stratified solves. BFF and OptCuts comparisons sharpen the scope: recutting can be faster and lower-distortion when allowed, while the neural solver targets supplied-chart validity and validation-first atlas construction. On Amara Spatial generated meshes, the full atlas construction path gives packed-atlas coverage on a 25-asset set and 1000/1000 strict locally valid atlases with zero UV flips in a large-scale Rust atlas run after fallback routing.

title: Robotic Nonprehensile Object Transportation with a Hanging Tray
comment: 8 pages, 11 figures. IEEE/ASME International Conference on Advanced Intelligent Mechatronics, 2026
summary: We consider the nonprehensile object transportation task known as the waiter's problem, in which a robot must move an object balanced on a tray from one location to another. In contrast to prior works on the robotic waiter's problem, which make the robot tilt a tray rigidly held by its end effector (EE), we use a tray suspended from the EE by ropes, such that it behaves like a three-dimensional pendulum. Some prior works have actuated the robot so that the EE simulates the behavior of a pendulum, because pendular motion reduces the shear forces acting on the transported objects, minimizing the sliding of rigid objects and sloshing in containers of liquid. In contrast, our use of a real hanging tray allows us to obtain the benefits of pendular motion while only actuating a 3 degree-of-freedom (DOF) mobile base, rather than requiring a full 6-DOF manipulator arm. Our experiments in simulation and on real hardware show that the hanging tray substantially reduces both sliding and sloshing compared to a static, rigidly-grasped tray. Furthermore, we integrate the hanging tray into an interactive robot waiter demonstration, which uses computer vision to identify people with a raised hand and visual servoing to steer toward them and allow them to access the tray.

AI.tldr: A robot uses a suspended tray (3D pendulum) instead of a rigidly held tray to move objects, reducing sliding and sloshing while requiring only a 3-DOF mobile base rather than a 6-DOF manipulator.
AI.motivation: Prior robotic waiter works use rigidly held trays or simulate pendular motion with 6-DOF manipulators. The authors aim to achieve the benefits of pendular motion (reduced shear forces, minimized sliding/sloshing) with less complex actuation using a real hanging tray and a 3-DOF mobile base.
AI.method: A tray is suspended from the robot's end effector by ropes, creating 3D pendulum dynamics. The system integrates with a 3-DOF mobile base and uses computer vision to identify people with raised hands, employing visual servoing to steer toward them for object access.
AI.result: Simulated and real-world experiments demonstrate the hanging tray substantially reduces both sliding and sloshing compared to static, rigidly-grasped trays. The system was successfully integrated into an interactive robot waiter demonstration.
AI.conclusion: The suspended tray approach achieves the benefits of pendular motion while requiring only 3-DOF actuation, demonstrating that complex 6-DOF manipulators are unnecessary for effective nonprehensile object transportation in this application.

title: AnisoLift: Anisotropic Latent Representations for Coarse Particle Liquid Enhancement
summary: Particle-based liquid simulation is widely used in graphics and physical modeling, but high-resolution rollouts remain computationally expensive. Consequently, many methods aim to recover fine-scale dynamics and dense transport patterns from coarse particle simulations. However, these methods typically rely on additional particle generation, which still incurs considerable computational overhead and leads to poor representation. To this end, we propose AnisoLift, a structured latent closure framework that augments each coarse particle with learnable anisotropic ellipsoidal components. This allows the model to capture directional local structure from the underlying high-resolution flow without introducing extra particles. Given a coarse simulation, our model predicts residual corrections to particle states to bring the updated state closer to the aligned high-resolution teacher. Our training objective jointly supervises particle dynamics and anisotropic geometric structure, encouraging both physical consistency and structural coherence. Extensive experiments show that our approach enhances coarse liquid simulations through improving fidelity to fully resolved flow behavior.

AI.tldr: AnisoLift is a structured latent closure framework for particle-based liquid simulation that augments coarse particles with learnable anisotropic ellipsoidal components to recover fine-scale dynamics without additional particle generation.
AI.motivation: Particle-based liquid simulation is computationally expensive at high resolution. Existing methods that recover fine-scale dynamics from coarse simulations typically rely on additional particle generation, which still incurs considerable computational overhead and leads to poor representation.
AI.method: AnisoLift augments each coarse particle with learnable anisotropic ellipsoidal components. Given a coarse simulation, the model predicts residual corrections to particle states to bring them closer to aligned high-resolution teacher. The training objective jointly supervises particle dynamics and anisotropic geometric structure, encouraging both physical consistency and structural coherence.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that AnisoLift enhances coarse liquid simulations through improving fidelity to fully resolved flow behavior.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully captures directional local structure from high-resolution flow without introducing extra particles, enabling more accurate and efficient coarse liquid simulation.

title: Failure Modes of Deep Multi-Agent RL in Asynchronous Pricing: Reproducible Triggers, Trace Diagnostics, and a Partial Fix
summary: We study two reproducible failure modes of deep multi-agent reinforcement learning in continuous-time pricing markets: (i) tacit cartel formation between competing DDPG agents, and (ii) actor--critic instability at high event rates. We instantiate both inside a single CT-MARL benchmark (Poisson-clocked price updates, observation latency $δ$, interior-optimum logit demand), show that synchronous DDPG agents reliably trigger Failure Mode 1 with collusion index $Δ= 0.69 \pm 0.11$, and quantify a partial microstructure fix: asynchrony alone cuts collusion by 48\% and adding latency drives it to a minimum of $Δ= 0.28$. The fix has clearly documented costs: it is partial ($Δ$ remains supra-Bertrand), it is non-monotone in $δ$, and it does not survive Failure Mode 2, which emerges as DDPG critic divergence at $λ= 5$ and corrupts the phase-diagram cell at $(λ{=}5, δ{=}1)$. We accompany the scalar collusion index with trajectory-level trace diagnostics that expose the within-episode signalling collapse and the post-shock non-recovery.

AI.tldr: The paper studies two reproducible failure modes in deep multi-agent reinforcement learning for continuous-time pricing markets: tacit cartel formation between competing DDPG agents and actor-critic instability at high event rates. Using a Poisson-clocked benchmark, synchronous DDPG agents reliably trigger cartel formation (Δ = 0.69 ± 0.11). Adding asynchrony reduces collusion by 48%, and with latency the minimum is Δ = 0.28, but this fix remains partial, is non-monotone in latency, and fails against actor-critic divergence at high event rates.
AI.motivation: Deep MARL in continuous-time pricing markets suffers from reproducible failure modes: tacit cartel formation between competing agents and actor-critic instability at high event rates. Understanding these failures and their interplay is essential for developing robust pricing algorithms.
AI.method: The authors instantiate both failure modes in a single CT-MARL benchmark featuring Poisson-clocked price updates, observation latency δ, and interior-optimum logit demand. They test synchronous DDPG agents, introducing asynchrony and varying observation latency to examine effects on cartel formation, and analyze actor-critic divergence at different event rates λ. They also employ trajectory-level trace diagnostics to visualize signalling collapse and non-recovery.
AI.result: Synchronous DDPG agents reliably trigger tacit cartel formation with collusion index Δ = 0.69 ± 0.11. Asynchrony alone reduces collusion by 48%, and with optimal latency (δ = 1) the minimum collusion index is Δ = 0.28. However, the fix is partial (Δ remains supra-Bertrand), non-monotone in latency, and fails against actor-critic divergence at λ = 5, which corrupts the phase diagram cell at (λ = 5, δ = 1).
AI.conclusion: The study reveals that while introducing asynchrony and latency can mitigate tacit cartel formation in continuous-time MARL pricing markets, the solutions are limited—collusion remains supra-Bertrand, the effectiveness is non-monotone, and the approaches fail against actor-critic instability at high event rates. The findings highlight the complexity of ensuring robust pricing behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning systems.

title: Efficient-WAM: A 1B-Parameter World-Action Model with Low-Cost Future Imagination
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. However, most existing WAMs rely on photorealistic future prediction, which incurs high inference latency and makes real-time robot deployment difficult. This motivates a more efficient WAM design that preserves the control benefits of future visual prediction while reducing its inference cost. We introduce Efficient-WAM, a World-Action Model that reduces the cost of future imagination while preserving its control benefit. Efficient-WAM improves inference efficiency via a compact video expert transferred from WAN-2.2-5B, token-sparse video latents, and asymmetric video-action denoising that allocates fewer sampling steps to video than to actions. Instead of optimizing the future branch for visual fidelity, Efficient-WAM treats future video prediction as a compact guidance signal for action generation. Comprehensive experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world manipulation tasks show that Efficient-WAM maintains strong action performance despite visibly coarse future predictions. While maintaining competitive control capabilities, our 1B-parameter model can reduce per-chunk latency to around 100 ms during physical deployment, achieving a 30x speedup over existing WAMs.

AI.tldr: Efficient-WAM is a 1B-parameter World-Action Model that achieves 30x speedup over existing WAMs by using a compact video expert, token-sparse latents, asymmetric denoising, and treating future prediction as guidance rather than photorealistic output.
AI.motivation: Existing World-Action Models (WAMs) rely on photorealistic future visual prediction, which causes high inference latency and prevents real-time robot deployment despite coupling future prediction with action generation.
AI.method: Efficient-WAM improves inference efficiency through: (1) a compact video expert transferred from WAN-2.2-5B; (2) token-sparse video latents; (3) asymmetric video-action denoising allocating fewer sampling steps to video than actions; (4) treating future video prediction as a compact guidance signal for action generation instead of optimizing for visual fidelity.
AI.result: On RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world manipulation tasks, Efficient-WAM maintains strong action performance despite visibly coarse future predictions. The 1B-parameter model achieves ~100ms per-chunk latency during physical deployment, representing a 30x speedup over existing WAMs.
AI.conclusion: Efficient-WAM demonstrates that reducing future prediction cost does not sacrifice control capability when future predictions are used as guidance signals rather than photorealistic targets. The model achieves real-time performance suitable for physical robot deployment while maintaining competitive control capabilities.

title: Deploying Speech-Driven 3D Facial Animation in Unreal Engine for Production-Ready Digital Humans
summary: Speech-driven 3D facial animation research has shown promising results, but most methods rely on representations that are not compatible with production pipelines. In this work, we present a deployable system that bridges this gap by enabling speech-driven 3D facial animation directly in Unreal Engine (UE) using ARKit-compatible representations. We construct 3DMEAD-ARKit dataset by converting the MEAD corpus into blendshape sequences using MediaPipe, and retrain FaceDiffuser and ProbTalk3D-X to generate stochastic and emotion controllable animations. We further develop a modular UE plugin with a Python backend that supports model selection, and parameter control. We compare the results to two existing commercial tools: Epic Games' MetaHuman speech-driven animator and Nvidia Audio2Face with a perceptual user study. The results highlight the importance of comparisons among academic and commercial pipelines. We recommend watching the supplementary video. We also plan to do live demonstrations of our work at Siggraph 2026 conference.

AI.tldr: A deployable system for speech-driven 3D facial animation in Unreal Engine using ARKit-compatible representations, featuring dataset construction, model retraining, and a modular UE plugin with comparison against commercial tools.
AI.motivation: Most speech-driven 3D facial animation methods use representations incompatible with production pipelines, creating a gap between academic research and commercial applications.
AI.method: Constructed 3DMEAD-ARKit dataset by converting MEAD corpus to blendshape sequences via MediaPipe; retrained FaceDiffuser and ProbTalk3D-X for stochastic and emotion-controllable animations; developed a modular UE plugin with Python backend supporting model selection and parameter control.
AI.result: Successfully created a deployable system enabling speech-driven 3D facial animation directly in Unreal Engine using ARKit-compatible representations; conducted perceptual user study comparing results with Epic Games' MetaHuman and Nvidia Audio2Face.
AI.conclusion: The system effectively bridges the gap between academic research and production pipelines, demonstrating the importance of comparing academic and commercial approaches. Future plans include live demonstrations at SIGGRAPH 2026.

title: Decoupling Thought from Speech: Knowledge-Grounded Counterfactual Reasoning for Resilient Multi-Agent Argumentation
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 30th International Conference on Knowledge-Based and Intelligent Information & Engineering Systems (KES 2026)
summary: Multi-agent debate frameworks have been shown to improve large language model performance in convergent tasks, but they are currently optimized in a way that heavily favors final output accuracy rather than stability of the process. During long-horizon exchanges reactive systems under sustained perturbations often experience logic degradation, argument repetition, and role drift. To structurally prevent the identity loss and maintain the process fidelity, we introduce Knowledge-Grounded Counterfactual Reasoning (KG-CFR), a dual-stage architecture that enforces a strict separation of concerns between a private, retrieval-augmented planning buffer, and a public execution layer. We assess this system in Dynamic Resource Allocation under Uncertainty (DRAU), a dedicated 1v1v1 environment, introducing diversity as distinct from standard debate settings. Over 270 completely factorial crisis simulation trajectories with stochastic environmental shocks, KG-CFR prevents judge-detected critical post-shock degradation (defined as a quality shift, $Δ\le -0.20$) in more than 95% of perturbed runs, increasing the overall argument quality from 0.694 to 0.822. Our primary contribution is the demonstration of architectural decoupling being an important factor of systemic resilience enhancement under sustained pressure without quality loss. Furthermore, we introduce custom vector metrics for discourse divergence and plan-execution alignment that provide strong, directionally consistent evidence of operational stability. Our ablation experiments suggest that the proper doctrinal grounding can be an equally important factor for argument quality, as the prospective planning. KG-CFR, according to our initial metric evaluations, reduces semantic looping, by preserving the agent's consistency with the original plan.

AI.tldr: KG-CFR is a dual-stage architecture that separates planning and execution in multi-agent debate systems, improving stability and argument quality in dynamic resource allocation tasks.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent debate frameworks optimize for final output accuracy but suffer from logic degradation, argument repetition, and role drift during sustained perturbations, requiring architectural improvements for process fidelity.
AI.method: KG-CFR introduces a dual-stage architecture with a private, retrieval-augmented planning buffer and a public execution layer, enforcing strict separation of concerns. Custom vector metrics measure discourse divergence and plan-execution alignment.
AI.result: In the DRAU environment (270 factorial trajectories), KG-CFR prevents critical post-shock degradation in 95%+ of perturbed runs and increases overall argument quality from 0.694 to 0.822, significantly reducing semantic looping.
AI.conclusion: Architectural decoupling is a key factor for enhancing systemic resilience under sustained pressure without quality loss; doctrinal grounding is as important as prospective planning for argument quality.

title: Flow Control: Steering Vision-Language-Action Models with Simple Real-Time Inputs
summary: We introduce flow control of vision-language-action (VLA) models, a simple and effective way to steer VLA actions in real-time through generic inputs, such as a keyboard. This method can be used out-of-the-box and does not require retraining or fine-tuning VLAs. It enables relatively crude user inputs to steer a VLA to align with user intent. The VLA transforms these inputs into action samples drawn from the VLA expert action distribution learned during training, so that the generated actions are high quality (conformity to the action expert distribution) and high fidelity (reflecting the user's intent). We demonstrate that flow control has many desirable properties: (1) flow control accurately and responsively steers robot actions with user inputs, (2) it is robust to suboptimal user inputs, (3) it enables users to steer VLAs to achieve significantly higher success rates and faster task completion, and (4) fine-tuning a VLA on flow control trajectories improves the autonomous policy. Together, these results provide a simple and intuitive way for users to help steer VLA actions, increasing task performance.

AI.tldr: A method for real-time steering of vision-language-action (VLA) models through generic user inputs (like keyboards) that generates high-quality, high-fidelity actions without requiring retraining, with benefits including improved task success rates, robustness to suboptimal inputs, and better performance after fine-tuning on flow control trajectories.
AI.motivation: VLAs often lack intuitive ways for users to directly influence robot actions in real-time. Existing methods either require complex retraining/fine-tuning or cannot handle crude user inputs effectively. There's a need for a simple, intuitive approach that enables users to steer VLA actions to align with their intent.
AI.method: Flow control transforms generic user inputs (e.g., keyboard commands) into action samples drawn from the VLA's pre-trained expert action distribution. This is done without retraining the VLA - the model simply selects actions that align with both user intent and its learned expert distribution.
AI.result: Flow control (1) accurately steers robot actions with user inputs, (2) is robust to suboptimal inputs, (3) enables significantly higher success rates and faster task completion, and (4) fine-tuning on flow control trajectories improves the autonomous policy.
AI.conclusion: Flow control provides a simple, intuitive way for users to steer VLA actions, increasing task performance without requiring retraining, and can even improve autonomous policies when used for fine-tuning.

title: SkillAxe: Sharpening LLM-Authored Agent Skills Through Evaluation-Guided Self-Refinement
summary: Skill documents, structured natural-language instructions that guide Large Language Model (LLM) agents, are critical to modern agent frameworks, yet LLMs struggle to write skills that actually work. On SkillsBench, human-authored skills improve pass rates by 16.2 percentage points, while LLM-authored skills provide no measurable gain. We introduce SkillAxe, a fully unsupervised framework that enables LLMs to iteratively diagnose and refine their own skills. SkillAxe decomposes skill quality into four interpretable dimensions (quality impact, trigger precision, instruction compliance with fault attribution, and solution-path coverage), producing structured improvement briefs that require no ground-truth labels, test suites, or environment rewards. On SkillsBench, SkillAxe improves pass rates by 28\% relative over unimproved LLM skills and closes 47--67\% of the gap to human-authored skills. We validate the approach as a continuous improvement engine in the wild on SpreadsheetBench, where a SkillAxe-built skill library learns from past agent trajectories and raises pass rate from 16.0\% to 52.0\% using only 22 skills.

AI.tldr: SkillAxe is an unsupervised framework enabling LLM agents to iteratively diagnose and refine their own skills by decomposing quality into four interpretable dimensions, achieving 28% relative improvement over unimproved LLM skills and closing 47-67% of the gap to human-authored skills on SkillsBench.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle to write effective skill documents (structured natural-language instructions for agent frameworks). On SkillsBench, human-authored skills improve pass rates by 16.2 percentage points over LLM-authored skills, which provide no measurable gain.
AI.method: SkillAxe is a fully unsupervised framework enabling LLMs to iteratively diagnose and refine their own skills. It decomposes skill quality into four interpretable dimensions: quality impact, trigger precision, instruction compliance with fault attribution, and solution-path coverage. The framework produces structured improvement briefs without requiring ground-truth labels, test suites, or environment rewards.
AI.result: On SkillsBench, SkillAxe improves pass rates by 28% relative over unimproved LLM skills and closes 47-67% of the gap to human-authored skills. On SpreadsheetBench, a SkillAxe-built skill library learning from past agent trajectories raised pass rate from 16.0% to 52.0% using only 22 skills.
AI.conclusion: SkillAxe demonstrates that LLMs can effectively self-improve their skills through iterative diagnosis and refinement, achieving significant performance gains without supervision and bridging substantial portions of the performance gap to human-authored skills.

title: Exploration of Foundation Model-Based Robots in Patient and Elderly Care
summary: Demand for older-adult and patient care is growing rapidly as populations age worldwide. Foundation models are increasingly being integrated into robots and interactive agents, with the promise of more flexible communication and personalized assistance. However, care settings require reliable and workflow-compatible systems with accountable human oversight, and it remains unclear whether current embodied systems can translate technical advances into clinical impact. This Perspective synthesizes foundation model-based care robots across three areas: design features, user experience, and evidence for care-related outcomes. Current systems most commonly use foundation models as conversational and reasoning layers within voice-centered socially assistive embodiments, while multimodal grounding and physical autonomy remain limited. Empirical evaluations report positive usability and engagement benefits, but reliability failures persist across the interaction pipeline such as hallucinations and conversational breakdowns. Evidence for care impact remains concentrated in proximal outcomes such as cognitive engagement and participation, with limited evidence for validated clinical or care-related changes. We argue that future research should transition toward care-specific evaluation standards, accountable autonomy, and integration into care workflows to support more responsive and responsible care technologies.

AI.tldr: This perspective synthesizes foundation model-based care robots across design features, user experience, and care outcomes, finding that current systems show promise in usability and engagement but suffer from reliability failures and lack robust evidence for clinical impact.
AI.motivation: As populations age worldwide, demand for older-adult and patient care grows rapidly. Foundation models are being integrated into robots and interactive agents for more flexible communication and personalized assistance, but care settings require reliable, workflow-compatible systems with accountable human oversight. There is uncertainty whether current embodied systems can translate technical advances into clinical impact.
AI.method: This is a perspective paper that synthesizes foundation model-based care robots across three areas: design features, user experience, and evidence for care-related outcomes.
AI.result: Current systems primarily use foundation models as conversational and reasoning layers within voice-centered socially assistive embodiments; multimodal grounding and physical autonomy remain limited. Empirical evaluations report positive usability and engagement benefits, but reliability failures (hallucinations, conversational breakdowns) persist. Evidence for care impact is concentrated in proximal outcomes (cognitive engagement, participation) with limited evidence for validated clinical or care-related changes.
AI.conclusion: Future research should transition toward care-specific evaluation standards, accountable autonomy, and integration into care workflows to support more responsive and responsible care technologies.

title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Shared Context
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can scale large language model reasoning at test time by decomposing complex problems into parallel subtasks. However, most existing MAS rely on centralized orchestration, where a main agent assigns work, collects outputs, and merges results. As the number of subtasks grows, this controller becomes a communication and integration bottleneck. We propose Decentralized Language Models (DeLM), a MAS framework that decentralizes coordination through parallel agents, a shared verified context, and a task queue. Agents asynchronously claim subtasks, read accumulated progress, perform local reasoning, and write back compact verified updates. The shared context acts as a common communication substrate, enabling agents to build on one another's verified progress without routing every update through a central controller. Empirically, DeLM improves both software-engineering test-time scaling and long-context reasoning. On SWE-bench Verified, DeLM achieves the best performance across Avg.@1, Pass@2, and Pass@4, with gains of up to 10.5 percentage points over the strongest baseline, while reducing cost per task by roughly 50%. On LongBench-v2 Multi-Doc QA, DeLM achieves the highest average accuracy across four frontier model families, improving over the strongest baseline by up to 5.7 percentage points. The code is available on our project website at https://yuzhenmao.github.io/DeLM/.

AI.tldr: DeLM introduces a decentralized multi-agent framework for large language model reasoning, eliminating centralized bottlenecks through parallel agents, shared verified context, and asynchronous task queues, achieving up to 10.5% performance gains on SWE-bench Verified and 5.7% on LongBench-v2 while reducing costs by 50%.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on centralized orchestration where a main agent assigns work, collects outputs, and merges results. As the number of subtasks grows, this controller becomes a communication and integration bottleneck, limiting scalability for large language model test-time reasoning.
AI.method: DeLM decentralizes coordination through three core components: (1) parallel agents that asynchronously claim subtasks from a shared task queue, (2) a shared verified context that serves as a common communication substrate, and (3) a verification mechanism where agents perform local reasoning and write back compact verified updates rather than routing everything through a central controller.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, DeLM achieves the best performance across Avg.@1, Pass@2, and Pass@4, with up to 10.5 percentage points improvement over the strongest baseline while reducing cost per task by ~50%. On LongBench-v2 Multi-Doc QA, DeLM attains the highest average accuracy across four frontier model families, improving over the strongest baseline by up to 5.7 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: DeLM successfully demonstrates that decentralizing multi-agent coordination through shared verified context and asynchronous task processing eliminates the communication bottleneck of centralized orchestration, enabling both more efficient and more accurate test-time scaling for large language model reasoning, particularly in software engineering tasks and long-context multi-document question answering.

title: What Demonstration Curation Metrics Do to Your Policy
summary: We study whether demonstration-curation metrics that detect defective training episodes also improve the downstream behavior-cloning policy that trains on the curated data. On a contact-rich LIBERO pick-and-place benchmark with a controlled structural defect (early gripper release during the carry phase), we find that the two quantities are sharply decoupled. The metric with the highest defect-detection AUROC (0.804) produces the worst curated policy (13.3% task success), while a metric with a substantially lower AUROC (0.638) produces a policy that nearly matches the oracle trained on ground-truth clean data (90.0% vs. 93.3%). We further show that five of the seven metrics we evaluate exploit episode length as a trivial proxy for the defect label, a confound that inflates reported AUROCs to near-perfect values and disappears once episode length is controlled. Across all conditions, the contaminated baseline succeeds on only 3.3% of rollouts, and the two best curation methods close this to within 3 percentage points of the 93.3% oracle ceiling. Our results argue that curation methods should be evaluated by the policy they produce, not the defects they flag, and that any curation benchmark must control for episode length before reporting detection accuracy. We release the testbed, all metric implementations, and the evaluation pipeline.

AI.tldr: The study finds that demonstration-curation metrics for detecting defective robot training episodes are poorly correlated with the downstream policy performance they aim to improve. On a LIBERO pick-and-place benchmark, the metric with the highest defect-detection AUROC (0.804) produced a policy with only 13.3% success, while a lower-performing metric (0.638 AUROC) achieved 90% success, nearly matching an oracle trained on clean data. Many metrics exploit episode length as a trivial proxy for defects, inflating detection accuracy.
AI.motivation: Demonstration-curation metrics claim to improve robot learning by filtering out defective training episodes, but there's uncertainty whether better defect detection actually leads to better downstream policies. The authors aim to investigate this relationship and expose potential confounds in current benchmarking approaches.
AI.method: The authors evaluate seven demonstration-curation metrics on a LIBERO contact-rich pick-and-place benchmark with controlled structural defects (early gripper release). They measure both defect-detection AUROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve) and downstream policy success rates. They analyze whether metrics exploit episode length as a proxy for defects and examine the correlation between detection performance and policy improvement.
AI.result: Defect-detection metrics and policy performance are sharply decoupled. The best detection metric (0.804 AUROC) produced the worst policy (13.3% success). A lower-performing metric (0.638 AUROC) achieved 90% success, nearly matching the oracle (93.3%). Five of seven metrics exploited episode length as a proxy for defects, inflating AUROCs. Contaminated baseline achieved only 3.3% success; best curation methods closed this gap to within 3 percentage points of the oracle.
AI.conclusion: Curation methods should be evaluated by the policies they produce, not the defects they flag. Any curation benchmark must control for episode length before reporting detection accuracy. The study provides a testbed with metric implementations and evaluation pipeline to enable more reliable benchmarking of demonstration-curation approaches.

title: LLM-Mediated Demand Response Coordination in Smart Microgrids
comment: Accepted for publication in 18th International Conference on Sustainability in Energy and Buildings (SEB-26), to appear in Springer Nature proceedings (KES Smart Innovation Systems and Technologies). The final authenticated version will be available online at Springer
summary: Effective demand response in smart microgrids requires prosumers to cooperate voluntarily under strategic self-interest, a coordination problem structurally equivalent to a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma on a social network. This paper presents a multi-agent simulation in which a Large Language Model (LLM) Influence Compiler issues structured demand-response directives to a population of heterogeneous prosumer agents, each governed by a hybrid decision architecture combining game-theoretic base probability (derived from payoff history, neighbour imitation, and exploitation memory) with LLM narrative evaluation of incoming coordination signals. The hybrid architecture resolves a key methodological challenge: LLMs aligned via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) exhibit strong cooperation bias when used as direct decision-makers, producing flat dynamics regardless of grid conditions. By separating strategic reasoning from grounded narrative evaluation, the model generates realistic prosumer behaviour across six personality archetypes, with baseline cooperation near 50% and clear differentiation under influence. Compiled structured directives achieve 33.3% demand-curtailment cooperation versus 27.0% for unstructured messaging and 28.0% for a no-intervention baseline ($Δ_\mathrm{comp} = +0.063$), with the advantage preserved across both grounded and idealized agent substrates ($Δ= +0.083$) and across all resistance levels ($R = 0.1$ to $0.7$). Hub-targeted dissemination via high-centrality network nodes outperforms peripheral or random targeting, confirming that grid topology provides mechanistic amplification independent of message content. These results suggest that structured LLM compilation, grounded agent reasoning, and network-aware targeting are complementary design principles for scalable, interpretable demand-response coordination in smart-city energy systems.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent simulation uses an LLM Influence Compiler to send structured demand-response directives to heterogeneous prosumer agents. The agents employ a hybrid decision architecture combining game-theoretic base probability with LLM narrative evaluation, resolving the issue of LLMs having cooperation bias when used directly. Structured directives achieve 33.3% demand-curtailment cooperation versus 27.0% for unstructured messaging and 28.0% for no-intervention baseline, with advantages preserved across all resistance levels and agent substrates.
AI.motivation: Effective demand response requires voluntary cooperation from prosumers under strategic self-interest, structurally equivalent to a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma. A key methodological challenge exists: LLMs aligned via RLHF exhibit strong cooperation bias when used as direct decision-makers, producing flat dynamics regardless of grid conditions. The authors seek to separate strategic reasoning from grounded narrative evaluation to enable realistic prosumer behavior across different personality archetypes.
AI.method: Multi-agent simulation with LLM Influence Compiler issuing structured demand-response directives to heterogeneous prosumer agents. Agents use a hybrid decision architecture combining game-theoretic base probability (derived from payoff history, neighbour imitation, and exploitation memory) with LLM narrative evaluation. Six personality archetypes are implemented. Hub-targeted dissemination via high-centrality network nodes is compared against peripheral or random targeting.
AI.result: Structured directives achieve 33.3% demand-curtailment cooperation versus 27.0% for unstructured messaging and 28.0% for no-intervention baseline (Δ_comp = +0.063). The advantage is preserved across both grounded and idealized agent substrates (Δ = +0.083) and across all resistance levels (R = 0.1 to 0.7). Hub-targeted dissemination outperforms peripheral or random targeting, confirming network topology provides mechanistic amplification independent of message content. Baseline cooperation is near 50%.
AI.conclusion: Structured LLM compilation, grounded agent reasoning, and network-aware targeting are complementary design principles for scalable, interpretable demand-response coordination in smart-city energy systems. The hybrid architecture successfully resolves the cooperation bias issue in LLM-based decision-making by separating strategic reasoning from grounded narrative evaluation, enabling realistic behavior across different personality archetypes.

title: YUBI: Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation at Scale
summary: We introduce Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface (YUBI), a finger-aligned gripper designed to enable intuitive, ergonomic, and scalable data collection for bimanual dexterous manipulation. While handheld data collection systems such as Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enable affordable data collection, their bulky pistol-grip designs can pose ergonomic and usability challenges for fine-grained, dexterous manipulation tasks. To address this, YUBI presents a distinct design principle: yielding, finger-driven actuation that directly maps human finger movements to gripper jaw motion. Using the YUBI devices, we set up a data collection system with integrated VR-based 6 DoF tracking of the gripper, ensuring high-fidelity trajectory data acquisition. We curate a UMI-based dataset of unprecedented scale: 8,434 hours across 1.20M episodes and 119 tasks. Experiments show that YUBI offers advantages over the UMI gripper in versatility for complex bimanual tasks, dexterity, and operational efficiency. A single policy trained on the YUBI dataset transfers across multiple bimanual robots (UR, Franka, and ELEY) simply by mounting the gripper on each platform, confirming that the collected data are directly executable as policy supervision. We release the gripper hardware, data-collection software, and dataset as one integrated stack, offering the open community a reproducible path to large-scale data acquisition for advancing robotic foundation models.

AI.tldr: YUBI is a finger-aligned gripper with yielding, finger-driven actuation that enables ergonomic, large-scale bimanual dexterous manipulation data collection. It provides superior versatility, dexterity, and transferability across multiple robot platforms compared to UMI.
AI.motivation: Existing handheld data collection systems like UMI have bulky pistol-grip designs that pose ergonomic and usability challenges for fine-grained, dexterous manipulation tasks, limiting data collection for robotic foundation models.
AI.method: YUBI introduces a yielding, finger-driven actuation design where human finger movements directly map to gripper jaw motion. A data collection system with integrated VR-based 6 DoF tracking of the gripper enables high-fidelity trajectory data acquisition. The system creates a UMI-based dataset of 8,434 hours across 1.20M episodes and 119 tasks.
AI.result: YUBI demonstrates advantages over UMI in versatility for complex bimanual tasks, dexterity, and operational efficiency. A single policy trained on YUBI dataset successfully transfers across multiple bimanual robots (UR, Franka, and ELEY) simply by mounting the gripper, confirming the data's direct executability.
AI.conclusion: YUBI offers a reproducible path to large-scale data acquisition through its integrated stack of hardware, data-collection software, and dataset, enabling advancement of robotic foundation models. The yielding, finger-driven design principle successfully addresses ergonomic challenges while enabling scalable, transferable dexterous manipulation data collection.

title: RocketSmith: An Agentic System for High-Powered Rocket Design and Manufacturing
summary: This work presents RocketSmith, an agentic system capable of the design, manufacturing, and optimization processes in high powered rocket development. The system enables the intelligent automation of software tools as to not only validate factors such as flight stability but also generate the parametric design components for the rocket assembly. A collection of subagents and skills enable optimization workflows of flight parameters via iteration in both zero-shot and human-in-the-loop workflows. With this system, four distinct high power rockets with various motor and assembly configurations were developed utilizing the unique design capabilities of additive manufacturing. These assembly components were fabricated using various FDM printers, manually evaluated for flight readiness, and flight tested at a launch event. From these tests, all rockets achieved a stable launched and two of the four rockets were successfully recovered in reflyable condition. Within the collected flight data, an 84% accuracy was achieved when comparing measured apogee to that calculated in flight simulations.

AI.tldr: RocketSmith is an agentic system for intelligent automation of high-powered rocket development, including design, manufacturing, and optimization processes.
AI.motivation: The need for intelligent automation of software tools to validate flight stability and generate parametric design components for rocket assembly, enabling both zero-shot and human-in-the-loop optimization workflows.
AI.method: The system employs a collection of subagents and skills to enable optimization workflows through iteration. It integrates with additive manufacturing capabilities and various FDM printers for fabrication.
AI.result: Four distinct high-powered rockets with various configurations were developed. All achieved stable launches, and two were recovered in reflyable condition. The system achieved 84% accuracy in comparing measured apogee to flight simulation calculations.
AI.conclusion: RocketSmith successfully demonstrates the capability to design, manufacture, and optimize high-powered rockets with high accuracy in flight prediction, showing practical utility for real-world rocket development projects.

title: What Matters in Orchestrating Robot Policies: A Systematic Study of Hierarchical VLA Agents
summary: Hierarchical vision-language-action (Hi-VLA) systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for complex robot manipulation, by using high-level VLM planners to decompose tasks into language subgoals executed by low-level VLA controllers. Despite recent empirical progress, there is a lack of unified design principles for these systems: existing Hi-VLA systems differ in how they choose and connect planners, controllers, mechanisms to switch between the two, and how observations and memory are represented in the planner. In this paper, we present a systematic study of Hi-VLA design for robot manipulation. We unify representative Hi-VLA agents under an options-style control framework and benchmark core design choices across short-horizon, long-horizon, and reasoning-intensive tasks. Our analysis distills practical principles for building Hi-VLA systems, showing how model choices and interface mechanisms jointly shape performance. Applying these principles yields a substantially stronger system than either flat VLA control or a naively designed hierarchy, across experiments both in simulation and on a real ALOHA robot. Overall, our results provide a foundation for building more capable, robust, and principled hierarchical VLA agents. More information and video at jiahenghu.github.io/hi-vla.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies the design principles of hierarchical vision-language-action (Hi-VLA) systems for robot manipulation, providing practical guidelines for building more capable hierarchical VLA agents.
AI.motivation: Existing Hi-VLA systems differ in design choices regarding planners, controllers, switching mechanisms, and observation/memory representations. There is a lack of unified design principles.
AI.method: The authors unify representative Hi-VLA agents under an options-style control framework and benchmark core design choices across short-horizon, long-horizon, and reasoning-intensive tasks.
AI.result: Applying the distilled principles yields a substantially stronger system than either flat VLA control or a naively designed hierarchy, demonstrated in both simulation and real ALOHA robot experiments.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a foundation for building more capable, robust, and principled hierarchical VLA agents.

title: Locomotion analysis of a quadruped interacting with the lunar granular surface
summary: Deploying legged robots in extra-terrestrial environments includes many challenges due to complex terrain interactions, energy, and thermal constraints. For effective mechanical design of a lunar exploration quadrupedal robot, careful consideration of motor torques, energy expenditure, and cost of transport is required. The lunar surface is composed of granular regolith, which impacts the locomotion of legged robots and their performance. Locomotion algorithms trained with rigid contact assumptions are also ineffective when applied to environments with soft contacts, such as granular surfaces, which can result in instability and poor tracking. In this report, the physical modelling of the granular lunar surface-robot foot contacts is applied to a simulation environment with locomotion trained using Reinforcement Learning. A comparison is conducted between the policy trained on rigid contact and soft contact environments, analysing the gait and locomotion performance metrics. The analysis demonstrates that soft contacts simulating regolith surfaces pose additional challenges for Reinforcement Learning based training, result in a qualitatively different gait, and increase the overall energy expenditure.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the impact of lunar granular regolith on legged robot locomotion by comparing rigid vs. soft contact environments using reinforcement learning training, finding that granular surfaces pose additional challenges and increase energy expenditure.
AI.motivation: Deploying legged robots on the lunar surface faces challenges due to complex terrain interactions, energy constraints, and the granular nature of lunar regolith. Existing locomotion algorithms trained with rigid contact assumptions fail on soft granular surfaces, causing instability and poor tracking.
AI.method: Applied physical modeling of granular lunar surface-robot foot contacts to a simulation environment with locomotion trained using Reinforcement Learning. Compared policies trained on rigid contact vs. soft contact environments, analyzing gait and locomotion performance metrics.
AI.result: Soft contacts simulating regolith surfaces pose additional challenges for RL-based training, result in qualitatively different gaits, and increase overall energy expenditure compared to rigid contact training.
AI.conclusion: The research demonstrates that granular surface interactions significantly impact legged robot locomotion and that training with soft contact physics is necessary for effective lunar exploration robots.

title: Hierarchical Policies from Verbal and Egocentric Human Signals for Natural Human-Robot Interaction
comment: We provide video demos and code in: https://project-edith.github.io
summary: For natural human-robot interaction, a robot must understand human intent expressed not only through language but also through nonverbal signals such as gestures and gaze. However, current robot policies rely on language instructions as the sole interface for conveying intent, leaving nonverbal signals unused and placing the full burden of communication. In this work, we present EDITH, a robot framework that captures the human's nonverbal signals through continuous streams of first-person view and gaze from smart glasses, and uses them alongside language instructions as inputs to the robot policy. Our hardware system streams the human's first-person view, gaze, and speech to the robot in real time, transcribing the speech into language instructions. To handle these rich but noisy signals, we design a hierarchical policy in which a high-level policy infers the human's intent and produces a sequence of subtasks, where each subtask is represented as a fine-grained instruction paired with a keyframe that grounds the intent in the scene (e.g., the frame where the human points at the target object). A low-level policy then executes these subtasks. In our experiments on human-robot interactive tasks, EDITH enables the robot to act on the human's nonverbal signals even when intent is expressed only briefly, and significantly reduces user effort to convey intent compared to using language instructions alone. Visit our project page for source code and real-robot demo videos.

AI.tldr: EDITH is a robot framework that captures human nonverbal signals (gaze, gestures) via smart glasses and integrates them with language instructions using a hierarchical policy, enabling robots to better understand and act on human intent with reduced user effort.
AI.motivation: Current robot policies rely exclusively on language instructions for intent communication, ignoring nonverbal signals (gestures, gaze) that humans naturally use. This places the full communication burden on the human and fails to leverage available nonverbal cues for more natural interaction.
AI.method: EDITH uses smart glasses to capture continuous first-person view and gaze streams, which are streamed to the robot in real time along with speech. The system employs a hierarchical policy: a high-level policy infers human intent and generates subtasks with fine-grained instructions paired with keyframes that ground intent in the scene, while a low-level policy executes these subtasks.
AI.result: EDITH enables robots to act on nonverbal signals even when intent is expressed briefly, and significantly reduces user effort to convey intent compared to language-only approaches.
AI.conclusion: Integrating nonverbal signals alongside language instructions creates a more effective human-robot interaction system, as demonstrated by the robot's ability to understand and act on intent conveyed through brief nonverbal cues and the reduced user effort required for communication.

title: MARCH: Model-Assisted Reinforcement Learning for the Perceptive Control of Humanoids over Sparse Footholds
summary: Perceptive bipedal locomotion over sparse terrain remains a difficult challenge: model-based methods are precise but brittle to uncertainty, while model-free methods are robust but struggle to discover the precise, constrained motions required for safety-critical locomotion where small errors can cause catastrophic failures. We propose a model-assisted reinforcement learning (RL) framework that combines both perspectives in three steps: (1) generate a safe reference trajectory using simplified models; (2) train a privileged teacher policy guided by a control Lyapunov function (CLF) reward built around the safe reference trajectory; and (3) distill the teacher into a vision-based student policy. We show that this model-assistance procedure produces physically grounded locomotion, improving sample efficiency, reducing the need for a complex learning curriculum, and achieving smoother locomotion behavior alongside stepping stone performance comparable to model-free baselines. We validate our approach in simulation and demonstrate successful deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot navigating sparse footholds with lateral constraints.

AI.tldr: A model-assisted reinforcement learning framework that combines model-based precision with model-free robustness for safe bipedal locomotion over sparse terrain, using a three-step process of reference generation, teacher training with control Lyapunov function, and knowledge distillation to a vision-based student policy.
AI.motivation: Perceptive bipedal locomotion over sparse terrain is challenging: model-based methods are precise but brittle to uncertainty, while model-free methods are robust but struggle to discover precise, constrained motions required for safety-critical locomotion where small errors can cause catastrophic failures.
AI.method: Three-step framework: (1) generate a safe reference trajectory using simplified models; (2) train a privileged teacher policy guided by a control Lyapunov function (CLF) reward built around the safe reference trajectory; (3) distill the teacher into a vision-based student policy.
AI.result: The model-assistance procedure produces physically grounded locomotion, improving sample efficiency, reducing the need for a complex learning curriculum, and achieving smoother locomotion behavior with stepping stone performance comparable to model-free baselines.
AI.conclusion: Validated in simulation and successfully deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot navigating sparse footholds with lateral constraints.

title: Improved Representation of Matrix Lie Group Operations through Tensor Notation
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures + graphical abstract, 1 algorithm, 4 tables
summary: Several recent papers have demonstrated the utility of using Lie groups within estimation problems, yielding improved accuracy and consistency. This paper introduces a new tool for describing operations with matrix Lie groups: tensors and the Einstein summation notation. While tensors and Einstein notation are well-known in other research fields, applying this mathematical notation to represent and compute matrix Lie derivatives is novel. More importantly, this new notation greatly clarifies the derivatives and operations necessary to work with matrix Lie Groups in (gradient-based) estimation frameworks. Therefore, the main contribution of this paper is not a new capability, but a more perspicuous mathematical notation for working with matrix Lie groups.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces tensors and Einstein summation notation to clarify and simplify operations with matrix Lie groups in estimation frameworks.
AI.motivation: Recent research has demonstrated the utility of Lie groups in estimation problems, but working with matrix Lie groups can be complex and unclear. The authors aim to provide better mathematical notation to make these operations more perspicuous.
AI.method: Applying well-known concepts from other fields—tensors and Einstein summation notation—to represent and compute matrix Lie derivatives, which is novel in this context.
AI.result: The new notation greatly clarifies the derivatives and operations necessary to work with matrix Lie groups in gradient-based estimation frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The primary contribution is not a new capability but rather a more perspicuous mathematical notation for working with matrix Lie groups, making the underlying mathematics clearer and more manageable.

title: SARM2: Multi-Task Stage Aware Reward Modeling for Self Improving Robotic Manipulation
summary: Fine-tuning vision-language-action (VLA) policies for long-horizon manipulation still relies heavily on behavior cloning, which requires costly high-quality demonstrations and keeps policies near the demonstration distribution. Reward models can reduce this dependence by reweighting demonstrations and providing dense supervision for on-robot reinforcement learning (RL), but they must be dense, accurate, and general. Existing methods fall short: task-specific stage-aware models are accurate but require per-task annotations, while general vision-language-model (VLM) reward models are broadly applicable but too coarse for fine-grained long-horizon progress. We introduce RM, a multi-task stage-aware reward model that combines an action-primitive-based stage estimator with a multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) value head to produce dense per-step rewards across manipulation tasks. Building on RM, we further propose SPIRAL (Self-Policy Improvement via Reward-Aligned Learning), an on-policy reward-guided framework that improves VLA policies from cheap autonomous rollouts. On a 10-task benchmark, RM reduces value-estimation MSE by 80% over the strongest baselines; when used in SPIRAL, it improves task success from around 50% to near-perfect performance on Folding Shorts (58% to 100%) and Cleaning Whiteboard (50% to 90%), showing that high-quality dense rewards are key to a stable robot data flywheel. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/sarm2.github.io/.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RM, a multi-task stage-aware reward model with an action-primitive-based stage estimator and MMoE value head, and SPIRAL, an on-policy reward-guided framework that improves VLA policies from autonomous rollouts using dense per-step rewards.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning VLA policies for long-horizon manipulation relies on behavior cloning, which requires costly demonstrations and keeps policies near the demonstration distribution. Reward models can reduce this dependence by providing dense supervision for RL, but existing methods fall short: task-specific stage-aware models are accurate but require per-task annotations, while general VLM reward models are broadly applicable but too coarse for fine-grained progress.
AI.method: RM combines an action-primitive-based stage estimator with a multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) value head to produce dense per-step rewards across manipulation tasks. Building on RM, SPIRAL is an on-policy reward-guided framework that improves VLA policies from cheap autonomous rollouts.
AI.result: On a 10-task benchmark, RM reduces value-estimation MSE by 80% over strong baselines. When used in SPIRAL, it improves task success: Folding Shorts (58% to 100%) and Cleaning Whiteboard (50% to 90%).
AI.conclusion: High-quality dense rewards are key to a stable robot data flywheel, enabling policies to improve from cheap autonomous rollouts rather than relying solely on costly demonstrations.

title: OMG: Omni-Modal Motion Generation for Generalist Humanoid Control
summary: Humanoid whole-body control has made significant progress in recent years, yet existing approaches remain limited to few-skill policies with heavy reward engineering, or motion trackers that are difficult to extend to new input modalities. We argue that the key to general-purpose humanoid control is to build a scalable brain, a module capable of reasoning with diverse conditioning modalities, atop a reactive motion tracking cerebellum, mirroring the hierarchical structure of biological motor systems. Two challenges arise in realizing this vision: acquiring a vast amount of high-quality data to achieve general purpose control, and equipping the generator with the capability to condition on compositional, extensible multi-modal inputs. We present OMG, which addresses these challenges with a meticulous data curation, filtering and labeling pipeline, as well as a diffusion-based motion generation backbone that conditions on language, audio, and human reference motions. Extensive experiments validate OMG as an omni-modal whole-body controller exhibiting state-of-the-art performance, model scaling behavior and efficient adaptation to new distributions and modalities, marking a concrete step toward foundation models for humanoid robots.

AI.tldr: OMG is a hierarchical humanoid whole-body control framework combining a reactive motion tracking cerebellum with a diffusion-based motion generation backbone conditioned on language, audio, and reference motions, achieving state-of-the-art performance and efficient adaptation to new modalities.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches are limited to few-skill policies with heavy reward engineering or simple motion trackers that cannot extend to new input modalities. The authors argue that general-purpose humanoid control requires a hierarchical structure with a scalable brain for reasoning across diverse conditioning modalities atop a reactive motion tracking cerebellum, mirroring biological motor systems.
AI.method: OMG addresses two key challenges: (1) acquiring high-quality data through meticulous curation, filtering, and labeling pipeline; (2) enabling compositional, extensible multi-modal conditioning using a diffusion-based motion generation backbone conditioned on language, audio, and human reference motions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments validate OMG as an omni-modal whole-body controller with state-of-the-art performance, model scaling behavior, and efficient adaptation to new distributions and modalities.
AI.conclusion: OMG represents a concrete step toward foundation models for humanoid robots, demonstrating that hierarchical brain-cerebellum architectures combined with diffusion-based generation can achieve general-purpose whole-body control across diverse input modalities.

title: Rethinking Embodied Navigation via Relational Inductive Bias
summary: Object navigation requires an agent to locate a target in an unknown environment through visual observations. Existing methods typically rely on open-vocabulary detectors or vision-language models (VLMs) to answer where to search, but often overlook what not to trust - which semantic cues are unreliable. Open-vocabulary perception is prone to systematic misleading evidence: false positives, outdated static priors, and repeated failed exploration due to lack of embodied verification, which contaminates mapping and decision-making. Such errors are rooted in structured object relations in real-world scenes. To address this, we propose DB-Nav, a framework that reshapes the search space via dual relational biases. It factorizes target-centric relations into an Activation Bias (propagates contextual evidence) and an Inhibition Bias (suppresses unreliable regions via perceptual confusion and action-level falsification). These biases are unified into a Relational Activation-Inhibition Exploration Graph that modulates frontier exploration values using online observations and failed accesses. Experiments on ObjectNav benchmarks show that DB-Nav significantly outperforms existing methods in success rate (SR) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), offering a lightweight, interpretable, and robust navigation framework without costly online VLM reasoning.

title: HiMem-WAM: Hierarchical Memory-Gated World Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a new powerful paradigm for embodied intelligence, learning action-relevant visual dynamics that significantly enhance generalization and robustness. However, existing WAMs still struggle with task-relevant memory in long-horizon robotic manipulation. To address this, we present HiMem-WAM, a Hierarchical Memory-Gated WAM that integrates motion-centric latent actions, high-level skill latents, and boundary-triggered memory updates. Specifically, we develop a hierarchical latent action framework that jointly learns low-level motion and high-level skill latents, providing structured temporal abstraction. Meanwhile, a boundary-aware memory gate writes compact task states at predicted skill transitions, enabling causal inference without test-time generation of future video or optical flow estimation. Evaluated on LIBERO, LIBERO-PLUS, RMBench and real-world tasks, HiMem-WAM shows that hierarchical latents improve robustness under deployment perturbations, and the memory module substantially benefits memory-dependent long-horizon manipulation.

AI.tldr: HiMem-WAM is a hierarchical memory-gated World Action Model that integrates motion-centric latent actions, high-level skill latents, and boundary-triggered memory updates to address task-relevant memory challenges in long-horizon robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing World Action Models (WAMs) struggle with task-relevant memory in long-horizon robotic manipulation, limiting their effectiveness for complex manipulation tasks.
AI.method: HiMem-WAM develops a hierarchical latent action framework that jointly learns low-level motion and high-level skill latents for structured temporal abstraction, and a boundary-aware memory gate that writes compact task states at predicted skill transitions, enabling causal inference without test-time generation of future video or optical flow estimation.
AI.result: Evaluated on LIBERO, LIBERO-PLUS, RMBench, and real-world tasks, HiMem-WAM demonstrates that hierarchical latents improve robustness under deployment perturbations, and the memory module substantially benefits memory-dependent long-horizon manipulation.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical latent action framework and boundary-triggered memory updates effectively address the memory challenge in long-horizon robotic manipulation, enhancing both generalization and robustness.

title: A Practical Recipe Towards Improving Sim-and-Real Correlation for VLA Evaluation
summary: Simulation has become an essential tool for evaluating and improving vision-language-action (VLA) policies, offering scalable, reproducible, and controllable alternatives to costly real-world robot evaluation. Recent simulation benchmarks have made substantial progress on realism and diversity, yet these platforms have not been widely adopted as reliable proxies for real-world policy evaluation. In this work, we investigate this issue through the lens of sim-and-real correlation. We conduct a systematic study across multiple simulation platforms, VLA policies, tasks, and perturbation factors, measuring whether simulated evaluation preserves real-world conclusions in terms of policy ranking consistency, performance correlation, and perturbation-wise failure patterns. This analysis allows us to characterize the limitations of existing simulators and identify what kinds of simulation signals are more aligned with real-world deployment. We further examine how users should exploit simulation for policy improvement, including when simulator-based finetuning is beneficial and how the amount of post-training data affects sim-and-real alignment. Overall, our work provides a unified framework for measuring, interpreting, and improving the usefulness of simulation for VLA policies, offering guidance both for simulator designers and for practitioners who use simulation as part of the policy development pipeline.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates sim-and-real correlation for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, evaluating whether simulated evaluation preserves real-world conclusions across multiple simulation platforms, policies, tasks, and perturbation factors.
